title: Roadmap 12: schema design and scaling
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: Normalisation trade-offs, online index builds, replica lag, expand-and-contract migrations, shard keys, consistent hashing, and multi-tenancy isolation models.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: When does denormalising (duplicating data to avoid joins) beat a fully normalised design?

options.text: On a read-heavy path where joins dominate and the copied data rarely changes.
options.why: Right: you trade extra write work and drift risk for cheaper reads.

options.text: When the data changes constantly and every copy of it must always agree with the source.
options.why: Many copies of fast-changing data multiply update work and anomalies.

options.text: When the main goal is to reduce total storage used.
options.why: Duplication uses more space, not less.

options.text: When you want the database to enforce foreign keys for you.
options.why: Copied values are not backed by a constraint to the source.

questions.explanation: Normalise by default for correctness; denormalise measured hot paths (counters, summary columns, materialised views) and keep the copies updated in the same transaction or by a job.

questions.prompt: Why would you run CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on a busy production table?

options.text: It builds the index without blocking writes, at the cost of a slower build.
options.why: Right: it avoids the lock that plain CREATE INDEX holds against writes.

options.text: It is faster than plain CREATE INDEX because it skips a table scan.
options.why: It scans the table twice and takes longer.

options.text: It lets the build run inside a transaction so it can be rolled back.
options.why: It cannot run inside a transaction block.

options.text: It builds the index on read replicas only, leaving the primary alone.
options.why: Replicas replay the index build from the primary's log.

questions.explanation: A failed concurrent build leaves an INVALID index that you must drop and retry. JSONB columns are usually indexed with GIN, and the same CONCURRENTLY option applies.

questions.prompt: True or false: after a user's write commits on the primary, an immediate read from an asynchronous streaming replica is guaranteed to show it.

options.text: True
options.why: Replicas apply changes after the primary commits, so they can lag.

options.text: False
options.why: Right: a lagging replica can return stale data.

questions.explanation: Route read-your-writes traffic (the user's own recent changes) to the primary, or pin the user to the primary for a short window. Synchronous replication reduces lag at the cost of write latency.

questions.prompt: During a rolling deploy, the first step runs `ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN full_name TO name`, then new app pods replace old ones gradually. What goes wrong?

options.text: Old pods still running keep querying full_name and fail until they are replaced.
options.why: Right: two app versions share one schema during the rollout.

options.text: The rename rewrites the whole table and blocks all queries for hours.
options.why: A rename is a metadata change and is fast.

options.text: New pods cannot read existing rows because the data is renamed too.
options.why: The data is untouched; only the column label changes.

options.text: Replicas diverge from the primary until the deploy finishes.
options.why: Physical replicas replay the rename in order and stay consistent.

questions.explanation: Use expand and contract: add the new column, dual-write, backfill in batches, switch reads, then drop the old column in a later release. Every schema state must work with both the old and the new code.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply about changing a live table safely.

options.text: A new NOT NULL column with no default breaks old app versions whose INSERTs omit it.
options.why: True: their inserts violate the constraint.

options.text: Expand and contract: add nullable, write both, backfill in batches, switch reads, drop later.
options.why: True: each step is safe with old and new code.

options.text: On Postgres 11 and later, adding a column with a constant DEFAULT does not rewrite the table.
options.why: True: the default is stored as metadata.

options.text: Dropping a column in the release that stops using it is safe because old pods exit instantly.
options.why: False: old pods keep running during a rolling update.

options.text: Backfilling millions of rows in one UPDATE is best, since locks are held briefly.
options.why: False: it holds locks and bloats; use small batches.

questions.explanation: Add NOT NULL later, after the backfill, ideally by adding a CHECK ... NOT VALID constraint, validating it, then setting NOT NULL.

questions.prompt: A multi-tenant orders table must be sharded. Nearly every query filters by tenant_id. Which shard key is the best fit?

options.text: A hash of tenant_id, so a tenant's rows share one shard and tenants spread evenly.
options.why: Right: single-shard queries and balanced load, though a huge tenant can still be hot.

options.text: created_at ranges, so each month lives on its own shard.
options.why: All new writes land on the newest shard, creating a hot spot.

options.text: The country column, so users sit near their region and low-latency reads are kept local.
options.why: Few distinct values give uneven, lumpy shards.

options.text: An auto-increment order id split into ranges.
options.why: The latest range takes all inserts and tenant queries scatter.

questions.explanation: Pick a key with high cardinality that matches the dominant query and spreads writes. Partitioning splits one table inside one database; sharding splits data across separate databases or servers.

questions.prompt: True or false: with consistent hashing, adding one node to a cluster of N nodes moves only about 1/(N+1) of the keys, whereas hash(key) % N would remap nearly all of them.

options.text: True
options.why: Right: only the keys in the new node's arcs move.

options.text: False
options.why: Modulo hashing changes the divisor, which is exactly what consistent hashing avoids.

questions.explanation: Virtual nodes (many points per server on the ring) give a more even spread. Without them, load can be uneven.

questions.prompt: A B2B SaaS expects 20,000 small tenants. Cost matters, but a bug must not let one tenant read another's data. Which isolation model fits best?

options.text: Shared tables with a tenant_id column and Postgres row-level security policies.
options.why: Right: low cost per tenant with the database enforcing isolation.

options.text: A separate database per tenant, so that everything is physically isolated and easy to back up individually.
options.why: 20,000 databases multiply connections, backups and migrations.

options.text: One schema per tenant in a single database, migrated separately.
options.why: Thousands of schemas bloat the catalog and every migration runs 20,000 times.

options.text: A separate server cluster per tenant for maximum isolation.
options.why: The cost and operations are far out of proportion for small tenants.

questions.explanation: Set the tenant per transaction (for example SET LOCAL app.tenant_id) and write policies using it. Table owners bypass policies unless you use FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and superusers and BYPASSRLS roles always bypass them, so the app must connect as a plain role. Database per tenant suits a few large or regulated customers.
